program_meta.sop_limit: VERBATIM from the CS Graduate Application Checklist: 'The statement of purpose must be no more than two pages in length, single-spaced. It will be submitted as part of the online application.' No word count is given. Two single-spaced pages is roughly 1,100-1,300 words at 11-12pt; do not exceed two pages.
program_meta.extra_essays: No separate diversity/personal-history statement is listed on the CS checklist. There is a required 'Supplemental form' inside the online application: 'List any publications and your website on this form and on your resume (CV).' A resume/CV is also required and must include publications. No stated limit on either.
program_meta.deadline_fall_2027: December 8, 2026 (CS PhD, Autumn 2027 entry); decisions February 2027. CS Master's deadline is also December 8, 2026; decisions March 2027. Application opens mid-September 2026. Knight-Hennessy Scholars (separate, for the Fall 2027 cohort) closes October 6, 2026 at 1:00 pm Pacific. Suggested TOEFL/IELTS test date: October 2026 (at least six weeks before the deadline). 'All application deadlines are final. Applications will not be accepted after the deadline.'
program_meta.lor_count: 3 - minimum and maximum. 'You must submit a minimum/maximum of three recommendation letters and they must be submitted through the online application system.' 'We recommend that at least two of these letters be from academic sources.' 'We do not consider letters of recommendations submitted via Interfolio.' program_meta.gre: Not required. VERBATIM: 'GRE. These are not required for PhD or MS applicants.'
program_meta.english_test: TOEFL or IELTS Academic required; Stanford institution code 4704 (no department code). Test must be taken no earlier than 24 months before the deadline. IELTS must be sent via the IELTS E-delivery service to 'Stanford University Graduate'. There is NO India-specific exemption named. Exemptions listed verbatim: US citizens/permanent residents; 'Applicants who self-declare their first language is English'; 'Applicants who earned a U.S. bachelor's, master's or doctoral degree, or international equivalent from a university where all instruction was conducted in English'; 'Applicants with two or more consecutive years of professional or educational experience in English, in the past 10 years.' An English-medium B.Tech from an Indian institution plausibly satisfies clauses 3 and/or 4, but Stanford does not say so explicitly - confirm with admissions@cs.stanford.edu before skipping the test.

program_meta.advisor_model: Admission is to the DEPARTMENT, not to a specific advisor. Best verbatim evidence found, from Ehsan Adeli's Stanford page: 'Admissions are decided by departmental committees, not individual faculty. If you are applying to a Stanford graduate program and wish to work with me, please indicate your interest in your application materials.' Advisor matching happens after admission; several labs run rotations for already-admitted students - MARVL (Yeung-Levy) explicitly lists openings for 'rotation PhD students (already accepted to Stanford)'. Practical consequence: name 2-4 faculty in the SOP, but do NOT expect cold email to move the needle (several groups explicitly say they will not reply to applicant email). Medium confidence - inferred from faculty pages, not from a single dedicated CS policy page.
program_meta.ms_research_access: Yes, but via application/forms rather than automatically. Ermon Group: 'If you are a current or admitted Stanford undergraduate or M.S. student interested in research positions, please submit this form.' MARVL (Yeung-Levy): openings 'on a rolling basis for ... a limited number of MS or advanced undergraduate students'; current non-PhD Stanford students must fill out an interest form. So MSCS students can and do join SAIL/AIMI labs, but access is competitive and not guaranteed, and the MSCS is unfunded. Whether a formal MS thesis track exists was not verified (the CS Masters page returned no usable content on 2026-08-28).
program_meta.notes: MSCS-vs-PhD reality check, as requested: (1) HARD CONSTRAINT - 'Applicants to graduate studies in Computer Science must apply either to MS (including HCP) or PhD, not to both.' You must pick one. (2) Stanford CS PhD is one of the single most selective CS programs in the world and admits overwhelmingly on demonstrated research depth plus letters from people the committee knows. Akshat's profile is unusually strong for an undergraduate (7 works, near-all first author, CGPA 9.56) but the works are in mid-tier venues (CVIP, SAGE Digital Health) rather than MICCAI/NeurIPS/CVPR, and the letters will come from outside the Stanford committee's network. On that basis MSCS is the more realistic route AT STANFORD SPECIFICALLY, with two caveats: the MSCS is unfunded (~2 years of tuition + Bay Area living cost) and there is no guaranteed MS-to-PhD conversion - internal transition happens but is competitive and requires a faculty advocate. RECOMMENDED STANCE: apply PhD at Stanford only if Stanford is a reach on a portfolio where funded PhD offers are being sought elsewhere; apply MSCS only if you can fund it and treat it as a two-year audition for a lab. Do not apply MSCS expecting an automatic PhD conversion. (3) RED FLAG - Daniel Rubin (Biomedical Data Science / Radiology) appears on many medical-imaging AI shortlists but is now EMERITUS and his lab has pivoted entirely to 'AI in Performing Arts' / opera; he is not a viable medical-imaging advisor. (4) RED FLAG - Stanford has heavy faculty outflow and dual affiliation with industry (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Physical Intelligence, startups). Ludwig Schmidt and Sanmi Koyejo both hold or have held outside affiliations. Re-verify every name in October-November 2026, immediately before submitting. (5) Several of the best-fit people (Yeung-Levy, Zou, Chaudhari, Langlotz, Adeli) sit in Biomedical Data Science / Radiology / Psychiatry rather than CS. If medical imaging under annotation scarcity is the real target, the Biomedical Data Science PhD or Biomedical Informatics (BMI) PhD may be a better-matched and slightly less brutal door than CS - those programs were NOT researched here and should be a separate task.

faculty.lab: Ermon Group (SAIL); Fellow, Woods Institute for the Environment
faculty.research_areas: Deep generative models (diffusion, flow/score-based, discrete diffusion), self-supervised and generative pretraining, transferability of pretrained representations, calibration and uncertainty, weak supervision, distillation and one-step generators, ML for sustainability/remote sensing.
faculty.why_match: Akshat's DDPM-pretraining work is a direct instance of Ermon's core question. Pretraining a denoising diffusion model on unlabelled BTCV abdominal CT and transferring the encoder lifted liver Dice from 0.751 to 0.928, and a FROZEN encoder retained 87% of the fine-tuned liver Dice - but the same frozen encoder FAILED on kidney (0.654 vs 0.899 for random init), i.e. generative pretraining bought representational structure for one anatomy and destroyed it for another. That is exactly the 'what does the pretext task actually teach, and to what does it transfer' question Ermon's group posed in SatMAE: Pre-training Transformers for Temporal and Multi-Spectral Satellite Imagery (NeurIPS 2022), and it connects to Generative Modeling Helps Weak Supervision (and Vice Versa) (ICLR 2023), which links generative modelling to label-scarce supervision. Akshat's kidney negative result is a concrete, unexplained failure case inside Ermon's own framework - a genuine research opening rather than a compliment.
faculty.key_paper_1: SatMAE: Pre-training Transformers for Temporal and Multi-Spectral Satellite Imagery, NeurIPS 2022
faculty.key_paper_2: Generative Modeling Helps Weak Supervision (and Vice Versa), ICLR 2023

faculty.department: Biomedical Data Science; by courtesy Computer Science and Electrical Engineering
faculty.lab: Medical AI and Computer Vision Lab (MARVL); affiliated with SAIL, AIMI (Associate Director of Data Science), and CERC
faculty.research_areas: Label-efficient and self-supervised learning for medical/biomedical imaging, vision-language and multimodal models for biomedicine, self-training, active learning, controlled ablation studies of representation learning, surgical and microscopy video understanding, flow matching for cell imaging.
faculty.why_match: Two of Akshat's results sit squarely inside MARVL's programme. (a) His semi-supervised SPIDER lumbar-spine pipeline trained a teacher on 54 labelled MRI slices (0.735 mIoU), filtered its pseudo-labels, and reached 0.816 mIoU with the student (+8.1 absolute points) - and, more interestingly, per-class confidence thresholds calibrated on only 5 reference images matched those derived from 304. That is the same annotation-bottleneck problem attacked in GLoRIA: A Multimodal Global-Local Representation Learning Framework for Label-Efficient Medical Image Recognition (ICCV 2021) and in Video-STaR: Self-training enables video instruction tuning with any supervision (ICLR 2025). (b) His diffusion frozen-encoder probe (liver retains 87% of fine-tuned Dice, kidney falls below random init) is precisely the controlled, single-variable representation-comparison methodology of Data or Language Supervision: What Makes CLIP Better than DINO? (EMNLP 2025 Findings), where her group held everything fixed to isolate one causal factor. Akshat's rigorous-empiricist identity - controlled ablations, reported negative results - is a direct methodological match to that paper.
faculty.key_paper_1: Data or Language Supervision: What Makes CLIP Better than DINO?, EMNLP 2025 (Findings)
faculty.key_paper_2: GLoRIA: A Multimodal Global-Local Representation Learning Framework for Label-Efficient Medical Image Recognition, ICCV 2021

faculty.department: Biomedical Data Science; by courtesy Computer Science and Electrical Engineering
faculty.lab: Stanford AI for Science Lab; member of SAIL; faculty director at Stanford Data Science Institute; two-time Chan-Zuckerberg Investigator
faculty.research_areas: Data-centric ML - data valuation (Data Shapley, Beta-Shapley, Data-OOB, OpenDataVal, DataPerf), dataset quality and dataset auditing, label/annotation quality, synthetic data and generative-model evaluation, distribution shift discovery, AI for health and clinical imaging.
faculty.why_match: Akshat's A-PDF work is an ad-hoc, hand-rolled version of the problem Zou has formalised. A-PDF generates augmentations with a conditional WGAN-GP and then REFUSES to trust the discriminator, instead scoring generated images against the class-proportion distribution of real masks (Mahalanobis retains 1,686/5,000 = 33.7%; kNN retains 1,757/5,000 = 35.1%) - i.e. an external, distribution-matched value function for synthetic data. That is the synthetic-data instance of data valuation as posed in OpenDataVal, Zou's unified data-valuation benchmark (NeurIPS 2023, arXiv:2306.10577), and it extends the Data-OOB / Beta-Shapley line. Second, Akshat's polyp study is a clean data-value-vs-capacity measurement: with architecture held FIXED and only preprocessing varied, the gain was +0.0453 Dice on U-Net, +0.0579 on ResU-Net and only +0.0226 on Attention U-Net - the value of the data intervention SHRINKS as the architecture strengthens. That is a directly publishable data-centric finding of exactly the kind Zou's group produces.
faculty.key_paper_1: OpenDataVal - unified benchmark for data valuation, NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv:2306.10577; listed under 9/23 news on james-zou.com)
faculty.key_paper_2: Data-OOB - out-of-bag estimate for data value, ICML 2023 (arXiv:2304.07718; listed under 4/23 news on james-zou.com). Related: Beta-Shapley, AISTATS 2022 (oral, arXiv:2110.14049).

faculty.department: Psychiatry & Behavioral Sciences; by courtesy Computer Science and Biomedical Data Science
faculty.lab: Stanford Translational AI (STAI) Lab (https://stai.stanford.edu/); also affiliated with SVL, SAIL, CNS Lab, PAC; co-director of AI4MH and the Stanford AGILE Consortium; faculty affiliate of HAI and AIMI
faculty.research_areas: Medical image analysis and segmentation, semi-supervised and weakly-supervised learning under annotation scarcity, diffusion/generative models for medical image synthesis and counterfactuals, evaluation metrics for medical generative models, multi-label diagnosis, confounder-free and bias-resilient representation learning, federated learning with partial labels, neuroimaging.
faculty.why_match: This is the single tightest paper-to-paper correspondence found at Stanford. (a) Adeli's Anatomical Similarity as a New Metric to Evaluate Brain Generative Models (MICCAI 2025) asks exactly what Akshat's A-PDF asks: how do you score a generated medical image for anatomical plausibility rather than trusting the generator? A-PDF answers it with Mahalanobis/kNN distance to the class-proportion distribution of 447 real masks (retaining 33.7%/35.1% of 5,000 cWGAN-GP samples). Two independent answers to one question - that is a real conversation, not flattery. (b) Adeli co-authored Medical Image Segmentation Review: The Success of U-Net (IEEE TPAMI 2024); Akshat's CVIP 2025 controlled benchmark of U-Net variants for lung segmentation reached the empirical counterpart of that survey's caution - no variant is universally best. (c) Adeli's own earlier line on Semi-Supervised Discriminative Classification Robust to Sample-Outliers and Feature-Noises (IEEE TPAMI 2018) and Multi-Label Transduction for Identifying Disease Comorbidity Patterns (MICCAI 2018) maps onto both Akshat's SPIDER pseudo-labelling (+8.1 mIoU points from 54 labelled images) and HiME's hierarchical multi-label decoder.

faculty.why_match: Chaudhari co-authored Self-supervised Learning for Medical Image Classification: A Systematic Review and Implementation Guidelines (npj Digital Medicine, 2023) - the reference synthesis of the exact question Akshat's DDPM study probes empirically. Chaudhari's more recent A Systematic Review and Implementation Guidelines of Multimodal Foundation Models in Medical Imaging (2025) shows the same evaluation-first instinct.

faculty.lab: Stanford Trustworthy AI Research (STAIR) Lab (https://stairlab.stanford.edu/); affiliated with SAIL, HAI, CRFM, AIMI, Stanford AI Safety, Machine Learning Group, Bio-X
faculty.research_areas: Currently: AI measurement science and evaluation, algorithmic fairness, robustness under distribution shift, privacy and federated learning, with applications to healthcare and neuroimaging. Historically: consistency theory for complex/structured output metrics, multilabel and multiclass classification, metric elicitation.
faculty.why_match: Koyejo's earlier line is the theory Akshat's HiME reinvented empirically. HiME composes per-level conditional sigmoids by the chain rule so a child's probability can never exceed its parent's, which makes the prediction set upward-closed and hierarchy-consistent BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by post-hoc repair - verified as consistency 1.000 across five backbones (ViT-B/16, ViT-L/16, ResNet-50, ConvNeXt-T, EfficientNet-B0) on Galaxy Zoo 2 (239,573 images, 37 classes, 4 levels, 95.8% decision-level accuracy) at ~0.01% parameter overhead. Koyejo's Consistent Classification with Generalized Metrics (arXiv:1908.09057, 2019) and Quadratic Metric Elicitation for Fairness and Beyond (arXiv:2011.01516, 2022) are the formal treatment of when a decoding rule is consistent for a structured/complex metric - precisely the missing proof scaffolding around HiME's Proposition 1. Akshat also has the honest negative to bring: under a FROZEN ViT-B/16 encoder, HiME scores 0.858 vs 0.888 for the flat baseline, i.e. the structural constraint COSTS accuracy at low capacity and is free at high capacity.
faculty.key_paper_1: Consistent Classification with Generalized Metrics, arXiv:1908.09057, 2019
faculty.key_paper_2: Quadratic Metric Elicitation for Fairness and Beyond, arXiv:2011.01516, 2022

faculty.research_areas: Conformal inference and distribution-free uncertainty quantification, selective inference and false-discovery control, active/prediction-assisted labelling and label-efficient statistical inference, knockoffs and feature selection, compressive sensing.
faculty.why_match: Akshat's SPIDER pseudo-labelling study made two measurements that are, in statistical language, questions about how many labels are needed to certify a selection rule: (a) he swept per-class confidence thresholding against Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty and found that combining the two adds nothing (MCDO 0.7910-0.7922, comparable to thresholding, no gain when merged); and (b) per-class thresholds calibrated on only 5 reference images matched those derived from 304. Candes's current programme is the rigorous version of exactly this: Probably Approximately Correct Labels (ICML 2026, arXiv:2506.10908), Optimized labeling resource allocation for prediction-assisted inference via OPAL (2026, arXiv:2606.03211), and Robust sampling for active statistical inference (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv:2511.08991) all ask how few labels suffice to give a distribution-free guarantee on a model-produced label set. Akshat's 5-vs-304 result is an unproven empirical version of a PAC-labels statement.

Akshat's efficiency-first framing (a spine segmentation pipeline built from 54 labels; a 56 FPS perception stack on a go-kart) fits that translational bias.
